1. Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose off the appeal filed against the order of conviction dated 17.12.2022 and order on sentence dated 21.12.2022 passed by Ld. ACMM01, Patiala House Courts,
New Delhi.
2. That on 05.11.2010, at about 11:30 AM, Food Inspector (FI) Sh. V.P.S Chaudhary alongwith Local Health Authority Sh. P.R. Jha visited M/s Jagjit Halwai, Shop No.4, Behind Hanuman Mandir, Seva Jagjit Singh vs . The State [Govt. Of Nct Of on 29 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105252888/
1 Nagar, New Delhi-110003, where the appellant/vendor was found conducting business of various food articles.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of "Coconut Laddu" lying in an open tray bearing no label declaration.
It is claimed that the sample of Coconut Laddu was taken as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act.

3. As per complaint, one sample of Coconut Laddu was sent to Public Analyst (PA) who vide his report dated 20.11.2010 found that the sample is adulterated because it contains added vegetable oil which is not declared as ingredient.

Accordingly, Sanction/Consent under Section 2 (ia) (a), (b) &
(m) of PFA Act, as punishable under Section 16 (1) (a) read with Section 7 of the Act was obtained and complaint was filed.
4. Summons were issued against the accused Jagjit Singh vide order dated 23.03.2011.

Accused/appellant has not exercised his right Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi)
2/10 under Section 13(2) of the PFA Act.

sentences.text: 5. A Notice for violation of provisions of the Act punishable under Section 16 (1) (a) of PFA Act, read with Section (a), (b) and (m) of Section 2 (ia) of PFA Act was served upon the appellant, to which appellant pleaded not guilty.

6. The prosecution examined 3 witnesses namely, PW1 Food Safety Officer Sh. V.P.S. Chaudhary,
PW2 Retired FA Sh. Shivji Mehto, and PW3 P.R. Jha, Additional Secretary to Chief Minister, New Delhi.
7. The statement of the accused/appellant was recorded under Section 313 Cr.PC in which appellant claimed innocence.
8. Record perused.
Arguments have been heard.
9. Firstly, in the present case, there was no public witnesses.

11. During the course of arguments, it was put to the Ld. SPP for the Department whether the key evidence and incriminating circumstances i.e. accused/appellant had disclosed the ingredients of the Nariyal Laddu (Coconut Laddu) on being asked by the Food Inspector and that in addition to the ingredients so disclosed, PA found vegetable oil in the said Nariyal Laddu (Coconut Laddu) was never put to the accused during the recording of Statement of Accused under Section 313 of Cr.PC.
12.

The Ld. SPP has not been able to give any satisfactory answer to the query of the court, except that the same is not relevant incriminating material to be put specifically in the statement under Section 313 of Cr.PC.
13.

In order to appreciate whether the same was required to be put to or explained to the accused, I had made certain additional queries, having seen the Hindi note of the accused on Form VI Ex.PW1/B. Ld. counsel for the accused submitted that the accused has only studied Hindi and did not understand English and that is why even in Form VI he made a note in his own handwriting in Hindi.

sentences.text: If this background was considered, the manner in which the statement under Section 313 of Cr.PC has been recorded, cannot be considered to be proper and fair.

Further, the entire case of the Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) 6/10 prosecution is that on the Form VI, the accused had only disclosed Coconut Powder, Sugar and Food Grade Colour as ingredients of the Laddu.

entities.text: Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He was being prosecuted as vegetable oil was found by the PA in the sample.

It was the non disclosure on his part which is the basis of his prosecution, as admittedly, the Nariyal Laddu is propriety food and had the accused disclosed the presence of vegetable oil at that stage, there would not have been any prosecution as the food could not have been called adulterated.
Therefore, this evidence and incriminating circumstance i.e. his non disclosure of all ingredients and the discovery of vegetable oil by the PA, was specifically, required to be put to him.

15. Now besides the factual error as noticed above, the Ld. ACMM has committed an error in stringing together all the evidence in the form of mere reference to exhibits instead of questioning the accused separately about each material circumstance intended to be used against him.

Reliance in this regard is placed upon the decision in Tara Singh Vs. State, AIR 1951 SC 44 and State of Karnataka Vs. Dashrath, 1991 Cr.LJ 2632.
16.

entities.text: Tara Singh Vs. State, AIR 1951 SC 44
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of Karnataka Vs. Dashrath, 1991 Cr.LJ 2632
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In Dashrath (supra), it was observed and I quote:
....
Often we find that a long series of facts are put in one question and the accused is asked to explain.
In one question several circumstances are included, and it may be that the answer to some of them may be in the affirmative while to the others in the negative.

The accused if he is not a very highly Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) 7/10 intelligent person with a sharp memory may not even remember all the circumstances put to him while giving his explanation.

entities.text: Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This may very often lead to miscarriage of justice.

In some cases, we have noticed that the examination is as general as it can be and questions are put to the accused in such a manner that it is difficult to make out as to what circumstance was intended to be brought to his notice for which his explanation was sought.
....The Court must question the accused in relation to all incriminating circumstances appearing against the accused.

Even if the accused was present when the witnesses deposed against him, the law still casts upon the Court a duty to marshal the evidence and to cullout all the incriminating circumstances and question the accused in respect thereof so that the accused may offer his explanation.
In a sense, the Court must also be satisfied that the accused has understood the circumstances appearing against him and gave whatever explanation he had in regard thereto.

The Law Commission in its 41st Report thought that the stage has not yet been reached for the deletion of Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) 8/10 this provision and may be in future, with better education and better facilities for legal aid this matter may have to be reconsidered in the charged circumstances.

As the law stands today, Sec. 313 of the Code provides not only the accused an opportunity to explain the circumstances appearing against him, but also the Court an opportunity to have a personal dialogue with the accused to elicit such explanation as he may have to offer free from the fear of being trapped to make an embarrasing admission or statement or of being led to make any statement meant to Jagjit Singh vs . The State [Govt. Of Nct Of on 29 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105252888/
5 fill up the lacuna in the prosecution case..... (emphasis supplied)
17.

The manner in which the Ld. ACMM has carried out the examination of the accused under Section 313 of Cr.PC and thereafter, proceeded to sentence the accused to simple imprisonment for the period of 03 months is a patent illegality/material irregularity, in view whereof, the order of conviction and sentence cannot be sustained and are set aside.

18. Therefore, the present appeal is being allowed and matter is being remanded back to the Trial Court for proceeding as per law from Jagjit Singh Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) 9/10 the stage of Section 313 of Cr.PC.
19.
